analysis.one_liner: Requires large online services and data brokers to disclose the value of user data and let users delete it.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its initial committee referrals and died at the end of the 117th Congress with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required large online platforms and data brokers — those with more than 100 million U.S. users — to tell each user, at least every 90 days, what data is collected, how it is used beyond the service itself, and what dollar value the company places on that user's data. It would have given users a single setting to delete their data, with narrow exceptions for legal or security needs, enforced by the Federal Trade Commission. It would also have required these companies to publicly report, in their SEC filings, the value of the user data they hold and of their contracts to sell or share it, so investors and the public could see how much of the business rests on data collection.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary users of large online platforms and data brokers' services, who would learn what is collected about them, what it is worth to the company, and could delete it. Investors would also get standardized disclosures of how much company revenue depends on user data.

how_it_helps.text: Requires commercial data operators to tell each user, at least every 90 days, what types of data are collected, how it is used outside the service, and the economic value the company places on that user's data.

Gives users a single-setting mechanism to delete all data a company holds about them, with exceptions only for legal obligations, legal claims, and fraud or security detection — and bars companies from retaining more than those exceptions require.

Requires large data-dependent companies to disclose in SEC filings the aggregate value of user data they hold and of contracts with third parties to collect or share user data, with the SEC developing a valuation methodology.
Makes violations enforceable by the Federal Trade Commission as unfair or deceptive practices.

analysis.who_pays: Large online platforms, social media companies, and data brokers, which would bear the cost of valuation, disclosure, deletion infrastructure, and FTC enforcement exposure.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies only to operators with more than 100 million unique monthly U.S. users, leaving smaller data brokers and platforms outside its requirements.

The SEC would have to devise methods to put a dollar value on user data, which the bill itself acknowledges may need to differ across sectors and business models — a difficult valuation task that could produce inconsistent or contestable numbers.
Deletion rights carry exceptions for legal obligations, legal claims, and fraud/security detection, so users could not delete all data in every circumstance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The user-facing rights (transparency about data collection and a one-click deletion mechanism) are a real but incremental privacy gain; the deletion exceptions and the 100-million-user threshold soften it. The SEC valuation disclosures are the more novel part — they would make visible, for the first time in standardized form, how much of a platform's business rests on user data — but that same valuation requirement is the hardest part to implement and the likeliest source of compliance disputes.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Financial Services committees and a consumer protection subcommittee, and neither committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Foster introduced the bill on March 17, 2022, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Financial Services Committee.
The next day it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce, and no further action was recorded.
No member of the House cosponsored the bill.
The 117th Congress ended January 3, 2023, without either committee holding a markup or the House voting on the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large online platforms and data brokers are better off, since they never faced the new disclosure, valuation, or user deletion requirements; investors also did not gain the standardized data-value disclosures.

for.name: Rep. Bill Foster
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Energy and Commerce and Financial Services committees.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral (chair: Rep. Frank Pallone, D-NJ)
against.what_they_did: Took no further action after referring the bill to its Consumer Protection and Commerce subcommittee; no markup or vote was ever held.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Additional committee of referral (chair: Rep. Maxine Waters, D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after referral; no markup or vote was ever held.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no opposition is on the record; the bill's support was a single House Democrat with zero cosponsors from either party, so the partisan shape cannot be measured.

industries.industry: Large online platforms and social media companies
industries.note: The bill would have forced them to disclose what data they collect, its value, and their third-party data contracts, and to build deletion tools for users — direct compliance costs and exposure for advertising businesses built on user data. Its death leaves their data practices undisclosed to users and investors.

Companies deriving material revenue from collecting, selling, or sharing user data would have faced the same 90-day disclosures and deletion obligations, plus SEC reporting of data contracts. The bill never took effect, so their practices continue unregulated by it.
